seo.title: Christmas Budget 2026: How to Plan It Without Debt
seo.description: Christmas 2026 is expected to cost about £1,681 per UK household and $1,654 per US household. Set your own budget, save weekly and avoid January debt.

h1: How to budget for Christmas without debt (2026)
summary: What Christmas is expected to cost in the UK and US in 2026, how to set your own number, how much to save each week, and how to avoid a January debt hangover.
intro_html:
Christmas 2026 is expected to cost a UK household about £1,681 and a US household about $1,654, according to estimates from MoneySuperMarket and Deloitte. This guide shows you how to set your own Christmas budget, save for it week by week, and pay for it without going into debt.

Those figures are estimates from surveys, not official statistics, and they vary a lot depending on what is counted. Some include food, travel and energy bills; others count only presents. Your own number matters far more than any average.

These are estimates from companies and trade bodies, not official statistics. The UK figure is a 2024 survey adjusted for inflation; the US figure is what people said they planned to spend before the season started. Because each one counts different things, they are not directly comparable, and other surveys give quite different totals.

Use them as a rough check, not a target. A household that spends far less than this can have a lovely Christmas.

The simplest Christmas budget is a short list with a number next to each line. Write it down before you buy anything.

  1. Gifts: list everyone you buy for, and put an amount next to each name. Multiply out: people × amount.
  2. Food and drink: the big meal, extra treats, drinks, and food for visitors over the holiday.
  3. Travel: train or plane tickets, fuel, parking, and getting to and from family.
  4. Extras: decorations, a tree, wrapping paper, cards and postage, outings such as a pantomime or a light show, and work or school collections.
  5. A small buffer: about 5% of the total for the things you forget.

Worked example

This is an example, not a recommendation. A UK family of four plans:

  • Gifts: 2 children × £60 = £120, plus 6 relatives and friends × £30 = £180. £300
  • Food and drink: £150
  • Travel to see family: £60
  • Extras (tree, wrapping, one outing): £60
  • Buffer (about 5%): £30

Total: £600. The same list works in dollars: just change the amounts to fit your own family and prices.

If the total is more than you can afford, cut the list now, not in the shop. It is much easier to agree a smaller gift with a sibling in November than to explain an overdraft in January.

sections.h2: How much to save each week
sections.body_html:
Take your total, subtract anything you have already put aside, and divide by the number of weeks left until 25 December.

Example: a £600 budget with 4 weeks to go is £150 a week (£600 ÷ 4). If you have already saved £200, it is £100 a week (£400 ÷ 4).

If that weekly amount is too high, you have three honest options: trim the budget, find the money elsewhere for a few weeks (for example by pausing takeaways or a subscription), or accept a smaller Christmas this year. Borrowing is the option to avoid.

Next year's version

Start in January and the same £600 is just £50 a month (£600 ÷ 12), or about £11.50 a week. That is a sinking fund: money saved in small, regular amounts for a cost you know is coming. Set up an automatic transfer for the day after payday into a separate pot labelled "Christmas", so you don't spend it by accident.

sections.h2: Cut the cost without cutting the joy
sections.body_html:
• Try a Secret Santa. In a big family or group of friends, each person buys one good present instead of many small ones.
  • Agree a spending cap. Suggest a limit, such as £20 or $25 a person, early. Most people are relieved when someone else says it first.
  • Give time, not things. Homemade food, a day out together or an offer to babysit often means more than another gift.
  • Plan the food shop. Write a menu, check what you already have, and buy for the days you will actually be at home. Christmas food waste is expensive.
  • Use cashback and loyalty schemes for things you were already going to buy, not as a reason to buy more.
  • Don't shop when tired or in a rush. Late-night scrolling and last-minute panic buying are where budgets break. Our guide on how to stop impulse spending has more tricks that help.
  • Keep the receipts and gift receipts in one place, so returns are easy if something doesn't fit.

Paying for Christmas with a credit card or "buy now, pay later" can feel painless in December. The bill arrives in January, when pay can feel a long way off and other bills are due.

  • Credit cards are only cheap if you clear the full balance by the due date. Carry a balance and interest is added every month.
  • Buy now, pay later splits a purchase into instalments. It is still borrowing. Several small plans at once are easy to lose track of, and missed payments can bring fees and affect your credit record.

How interest adds up: an example

This example uses an illustrative interest rate of 24% a year; your card's rate may be higher or lower. Put £600 of Christmas shopping on a card and:

  • pay £50 a month, and it takes about 14 months to clear, costing roughly £93 in interest;
  • pay £30 a month, and it takes about 26 months, costing roughly £174 in interest.

In the second case you would still be paying for this Christmas after the next one. If you already have card debt, our guide on how to pay off credit card debt faster explains the quickest ways to clear it.

In early January, while you still remember, write down what Christmas actually cost compared with your plan. Which lines went over? Which ones didn't matter as much as you thought?

Then start next year's Christmas fund straight away. Divide your new total by 12 and set up the monthly transfer before the January sales tempt you. A small, boring transfer every month is what turns next December from stressful into easy.

Be careful with the sales themselves: a discount only saves money if you were going to buy the item anyway.

sections.h2: Plan Christmas alongside your other bills
sections.body_html: Christmas is easier to afford when you can see it next to rent, groceries and bills. Add your monthly Christmas saving to the free SpendMath budget calculator to see how it fits. There are versions with typical amounts for the UK, in pounds, and for the US, in dollars. Your figures stay on your device.

faq.q: How much does the average family spend on Christmas?
faq.a: Estimates vary depending on what is counted. MoneySuperMarket estimates that a UK household will spend £1,681.12 on Christmas in 2026, including presents, food, energy and travel. Deloitte's 2026 survey found US households plan to spend $1,654 on the holiday season, up 4% from 2025. Both are estimates, not official statistics.

faq.q: How much should I spend on Christmas presents?
faq.a: There is no right amount: spend what you can pay for without borrowing. List everyone you buy for, put a number next to each name, and check the total against what you can save before Christmas. For reference, MoneySuperMarket puts UK households' spending on presents for family and friends at £187.16 for 2026.

faq.q: How do I save for Christmas in a month?
faq.a: Set a total, subtract anything already saved, and divide by the weeks left. For example, £600 with 4 weeks to go is £150 a week. If that is too much, trim the gift list, agree spending caps with family, and pause non-essential spending for a few weeks rather than borrowing.

faq.q: Is it OK to put Christmas on a credit card?
faq.a: Only if you can pay the full balance when the bill arrives. If you carry a balance, interest is added every month. In our example at 24% a year, £600 paid off at £30 a month takes about 26 months and costs roughly £174 in interest.

faq.q: When should I start saving for Christmas?
faq.a: January is ideal. Saving from January spreads the cost over 12 months: a £600 Christmas becomes £50 a month. Keep the money in a separate pot so it doesn't get spent on everyday things.
